extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of classical mechanics (advanced undergraduate / graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Use and application of D'Alembert's principle and the principle of vis viva (work–energy) to solve dynamics problems (examples: ballistic pendulum, wheel-and-axle, rolling bodies, chains). Emphasis on decomposition of forces, virtual displacements, moments and moments of inertia, and energy accounting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballistic pendulum kinematic/energy relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Relation between the horizontal velocity V imparted to a pendulum mass M and the subsequent amplitude/height of swing: the kinetic energy (vis viva) acquired from the impact is converted into potential energy Mgℓ(1 − cos α) (or V^2/2g = ℓ(1 − cos α)). Time of oscillation T and pendulum length ℓ relate via T = 2π√(ℓ/g), allowing determination of V from measured period and amplitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the period T and the amplitude (angle α or height h) of oscillation; use the trigonometrical reduction given in the text to compute V. Formulas presented show the dimensions consistency (gT factor has velocity dimensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballistic pendulum momentum transfer (simple centre hit)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a projectile of mass m and speed v becomes embedded in pendulum mass M and the two acquire a common velocity V after impact, momentum gives m v = (M + m) V (or, if m << M, v ≈ (M / m) V).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conservation of linear momentum for the impact to relate projectile speed to the pendulum's post-impact velocity; combine with the pendulum kinematic/energy relation to solve for v. Required observable quantities: mass of pendulum M, mass of projectile m, time and extent of oscillation (period and amplitude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-center impact: account for moment and point of percussion
rubrics_metrics.description: If the projectile strikes at a distance b from the axis (not on the centre), the moment of the impact force and the resulting angular impulse must be used: the angular acceleration and angular velocity produced depend on the moment bp and the lever geometry, and the vis viva generated is equated to the potential energy gain Mga(1 − cos α).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include distances of the centre of gravity and point of percussion from the axis, the masses m and M, and the time/extent of oscillation. Use moment-arm b to compute angular impulse (bmv/r etc.) and then equate rotational kinetic energy to potential energy to obtain projectile speed. The formula in the text exhibits the same dimensional structure as the simple-centre case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of impact forces and impulse (no instantaneous forces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the assumption of truly instantaneous (infinite) forces; impacts are modeled as very large forces acting over very short but finite time intervals. Replace instantaneous-force expressions by the impulse integral ∫p dt when necessary, so that m(v − V) = ∫p dt (or mv ≈ ∫p dt if V ≪ v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Poncelet's viewpoint: treat impulses as integrals of large but finite forces over short durations. If the active force during impact is not constant, substitute Cp dt for the simple product pτ; reasoning otherwise remains the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: D'Alembert's principle — decomposition of impressed forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose each impressed force P into an effective force W (the component that would produce the actual motion if the point were free) and an equilibrated force V; the equilibrated forces form a balanced system (balanced by constraints/connections). The effective forces W produce the actual motions of the connected system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label forces as impressed (P, P', ...), effective (W, W', ...), and equilibrated/gained-and-lost (V, V', ...). The equilibrated forces must be balanced by the connections; this decomposition is the core statement of D'Alembert's principle in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent forms: virtual displacements / virtual work
rubrics_metrics.description: D'Alembert's principle can be expressed as the principle of virtual displacements: the system composed of impressed forces P and the oppositely-signed effective forces −W is in equilibrium. Equivalently, the sum of virtual moments of the equilibrated system V (or of P − W) is zero; the elementary work of the equilibrated forces (neglecting strains in the connections) is zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this form to apply virtual-displacement techniques (Lagrange, principle of virtual work). It is particularly convenient to express equilibrium conditions of the system V or P − W using virtual moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical component method for D'Alembert applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve every impressed force P on a mass m into rectangular components X, Y, Z and every effective force W into corresponding components m ẍ, m ÿ, m z̈; resolve displacements into dx, dy, dz. The equilibrium (work) condition is Σ (X − m ẍ) δx + (Y − m ÿ) δy + (Z − m z̈) δz = 0 (or equivalently X dx + Y dy + Z dz = m(g dx + r dy + Z dz) for total work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express as many displacements as possible in terms of the remaining independent ones, then set coefficients of the arbitrary virtual displacements equal to zero to obtain the equations of motion (standard procedure for deriving differential equations via virtual work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statical moment and moment of inertia to get angular acceleration
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the angular acceleration of a compound pendulum or rotating system, divide the sum of the statical moments (moments of applied forces) by the sum of the moments of inertia. This gives the angular acceleration directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute statical moments (force × lever arm) and moments of inertia about the axis; angular acceleration φ̈ = (sum of statical moments) / (moment of inertia). This method often provides an alternative to the component/virtual-work approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limitation of D'Alembert's principle
rubrics_metrics.description: D'Alembert's principle reduces motion problems to problems of equilibrium by recourse to statical experiences and is a convenient routine-form; however, it does not obviate the need for detailed, case-specific mechanical knowledge or experiments. It supplies directions for employing previously obtained equilibrium experiences but does not add fundamentally new physical content beyond other formulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the principle as an economical method to apply known statical results to dynamics problems, but avoid assuming it replaces detailed mechanical analysis or experiments when those are required for insight or accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of vis viva (work–energy theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: The increase of the vis viva (kinetic energy) of a system equals the work done by the impressed forces: Σ p h = 1/2 Σ m v^2 (or, with variable forces, replace p h by ∫ C p ds). If initial velocities are nonzero, the theorem refers to the increment of the vis viva by the work done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply vis viva to compute velocities/energy changes when the total distance traversed and the force along each element are known. Replace discrete products by integrals for variable forces. Use this as an alternative to D'Alembert where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy accounting for rolling and composite bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: When bodies roll without slipping or contain internal rotating masses, the total vis viva is the sum of translational and rotational contributions; e.g., for a rolling cylinder with surface mass distribution, total kinetic energy = translational KE of axis + rotational KE of surface/masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute axis velocity u and rotational surface velocity v; sum 1/2 m u^2 and rotational 1/2 I ω^2 (or expressed as 1/2 Σ m v^2 for discrete masses). Use this sum with work done by gravity to get relations for accelerations (examples: cylinder with two opposite masses, uniformly distributed surface mass, or coaxial cylinders with different radii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vis viva without explicit path knowledge (central forces / conservative fields)
rubrics_metrics.description: For attraction to a fixed centre (central force) the increase of vis viva between two radial positions depends only on initial and terminal distances (r0, r1) and is independent of the form of the path; similarly for bodies attracted to several fixed centres, increases depend on projections along radii. Thus in many such cases vis viva can be applied without knowing the actual path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute work via radial components/projections; Euler's results justify replacing path integrals by differences of potential-like functions when appropriate. This enables solving certain dynamics problems purely by energy considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of vis viva to variable-mass/variable-length systems (chain example)
rubrics_metrics.description: For systems where the mobile portion changes (e.g., a chain partially hanging off a plane), apply the work–energy relation treating the variable mass and variable distance elements: the vis viva acquired v relates to the hanging length x by equating work done by gravity to 1/2 m_total v^2 (example gives v proportional to x for the chain problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up the work expression carefully accounting for the mass distribution (mass per unit length), integrate if necessary, and solve for v as a function of x. The same principle applies when forces are variable: use integrals ∫ C p ds.
